options: The exact number of seconds a program takes
How the work an algorithm does grows as the data grows
The number of lines of code
questions.explain: Seconds depend on the computer; Big-O describes the shape of the growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²)…
A set (or dict) jumps straight to where the item would be, whatever its size. In the lab, about 20,000× faster than a list.

questions.q: Binary search on 1,000,000 sorted prices needs at most about how many steps?
questions.explain: Each step halves what's left: 2^20 ≈ 1,000,000. Double the data and it costs one more step. The lab: never more than 20.

questions.q: For each of 20,000 orders, the code checks customer in past_customers (a list of 20,000). What is this?
questions.explain: An O(n) list search, done n times. Build a set once, then each check is O(1): 3.5 s → 0.01 s in the lab.

questions.q: An algorithm does 3n + 5 steps. In Big-O it is:
questions.explain: Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing part and drops constant factors.

options: Inside the loop, so it's always fresh
questions.explain: Inside the loop it's rebuilt every time: O(n) × n = O(n²) again (the mistakes/ example).

questions.q: (Going deeper) What does 'amortised O(1)' mean for list.append?
options: Every append takes exactly the same time
Now and then the list grows and copies itself (O(n)), but averaged over all appends each costs O(1)
questions.explain: Occasional expensive steps, spread over many cheap ones, average out to constant time.

questions.q: (Going deeper) A page shows 100 orders and runs one database query per order. What's this called?
options: The N+1 query problem: 101 round trips where one query would do
questions.explain: O(n) network round trips. Module 17 fixes it with joins and prefetching.
